c.tagline: Alpine lake city of diplomacy, watchmaking, and the soaring Jet d'Eau.

taxi.fareNote: Fares are among Europe's highest and always metered; book by app or use a rank rather than hailing on the street, and expect airport, luggage, and night surcharges.

emergency.note: 112 is the general European emergency number and reaches police, fire, and ambulance; 117 is direct police and 144 is the ambulance service.

avoid.reason: The Pâquis district near the main station has street drug dealing and petty theft late at night, and pickpockets work the lakefront in summer.

hood_desc: Geneva's medieval heart on the hill, a maze of cobbled lanes around St. Pierre Cathedral, Place du Bourg-de-Four, antique shops, and art galleries; best for first-timers who want history, sights, and atmosphere within walking distance.

The lively, cosmopolitan lakeside quarter behind the main station, packed with international restaurants, bars, and the famous Bains des Pâquis bathing pier; a walkable, sometimes gritty base for nightlife and cheaper eats close to everything.

An elegant left-bank residential district running along the lake from the Jardin Anglais past the new Eaux-Vives harbour and beach, with parks, boutiques, and a relaxed waterfront feel; good for travellers who want calm, greenery, and lake views.

A charming, Sardinian-built 'village' just south of the centre with pastel low-rise houses, leafy squares, artisan workshops, indie boutiques, and buzzing cafe-bar terraces; suits those after a bohemian, creative atmosphere away from the tourist core.

A student and alternative district around the huge Plaine de Plainpalais, home to the university, the twice-weekly flea market, farmers' markets, cinemas, and a young, arty going-out scene; great for budget travellers and market lovers.
lodging: The Ritz-Carlton Hotel de la Paix

water.note: Tap water is excellent Alpine-sourced and safe to drink everywhere.

transit.hours: Trams, trolleybuses, and buses run roughly 5:00 AM to around midnight; on Friday and Saturday nights the Noctambus network covers the late hours.
transit.pay: One unireso ticket covers TPG trams and buses, the Mouettes lake shuttles, and Léman Express and regional trains within the zone. A full 'tout Genève' 60-minute ticket is about CHF 3.00 (~US$3.40) and a short-hop 'saut de puce' about CHF 2.00; a day card is around CHF 8-10. Buy from machines at every stop or in the TPG or Léman Express apps. Guests of any Geneva hotel or hostel receive a free Geneva Transport Card covering all public transport for the length of their stay, and arriving air passengers get a free 80-minute ticket from a machine in baggage claim.

food.name: Fondue
food.desc: Melted Gruyere and Vacherin with white wine and kirsch. The Geneva twist adds tomato, which lightens it; bread cubes only, and do not lose one in the pot.

places.name: Cafe du Soleil
places.note: Four-century-old bistro treated as the city's fondue benchmark; book at weekends.

places.name: Les Armures
places.note: Old Town institution beside the cathedral doing fondue, raclette and rosti.

places.name: Auberge de Saviese
places.note: Valais-style chalet near the station, open late and good for a walk-in table.

food.name: Filets de perche
food.desc: Small Lake Geneva perch fillets floured and fried in butter with lemon and tartare. Ask for perche du Leman; many kitchens quietly use imported fish.

places.name: Cafe du Centre
places.note: Long-running brasserie with a terrace, known for perch fillets and lake fish.

places.name: Buvette des Bains des Paquis
places.note: Cheap, cheerful and right on the water; fillets served on paper plates in summer.

places.name: Restaurant Vieux-Bois
places.note: The hotel school dining room: serious classical cooking at friendly prices.

food.name: Longeole
food.desc: Geneva's protected pork sausage, coarse and studded with fennel seed, simmered slowly and served with potatoes, lentils or cardoon gratin.

places.name: Cafe du Soleil
places.note: Longeole, fondue and meringue with double cream can all be had in one sitting.

places.name: Cafe des Negociants
places.note: Carouge bistro strong on Geneva charcuterie and local wine by the glass.

places.name: Auberge Communale de Carouge
places.note: Chef-driven update of the Geneva canon in a handsome village-square inn.

food.name: Cardon epineux genevois
food.desc: A protected local thistle related to the artichoke, blanched pale under earth then baked in cream and cheese. Strictly a winter dish, around Christmas.

places.name: Auberge Communale de Carouge
places.note: Puts the cardoon gratin on when the Plainpalais crop comes in each winter.

places.name: Cafe du Soleil
places.note: Traditional cardon gratin served beside longeole in the cold months.

places.name: Restaurant Vieux-Bois
places.note: Seasonal Geneva vegetables cooked properly; ask what the winter menu holds.

food.name: Raclette
food.desc: Half a wheel of alpine cheese melted at the fire and scraped over potatoes with gherkins and pickled onions. Ordered by the plate until you stop.

places.name: Auberge de Saviese
places.note: Valais cheeses melted at the table; the easiest raclette near the station.

places.name: Edelweiss
places.note: Full alpine-chalet treatment with live folk music; touristy but genuinely fun.

places.name: Les Armures
places.note: Old Town setting for raclette if you want the historic room with it.

food.name: Marmite de l'Escalade
food.desc: Chocolate cauldron filled with marzipan vegetables, smashed every December to mark Geneva's 1602 victory. Chocolatiers sell them from late November.

places.name: Auer Chocolatier
places.note: Family chocolatier since 1820, a fixture of the Escalade marmite season.

places.name: Du Rhone Chocolatier
places.note: Geneva house founded in 1875; famous for its filled chocolates year round.

places.name: Stettler et Castrischer
places.note: Old Geneva chocolate maker, worth it for the paves even outside December.

food.name: Geneva wine
food.desc: The canton is Switzerland's third-largest wine region: crisp Chasselas, light Gamay and increasingly good Gamaret from vineyards inside the city limits.

places.name: Le Verre a Monique
places.note: Neighbourhood wine bar with a strong list of small Geneva and Swiss growers.

places.name: Cafe des Negociants
places.note: Deep cantonal wine list poured by the glass alongside bistro plates.

places.name: Cave Valaisanne
places.note: Old-school Swiss cellar restaurant for regional bottles with cheese dishes.

food.name: Local craft beer
food.desc: Geneva has a lively small-brewery scene, and the lakeside buvettes serve it in summer with the Jet d'Eau in view. Cheapest drinking in an expensive city.

places.name: Buvette des Bains des Paquis
places.note: Beer on the pier at prices Genevans can live with; open year round.

places.name: La Barje des Volontaires
places.note: Riverside kiosk bar, a summer institution for local beer and sunset drinking.

places.name: Cafe du Bourg-de-Four
places.note: Terrace on the Old Town's oldest square, good for a beer between sights.

landmarks: Jet d'Eau
Geneva's exuberant trademark rockets lake water 140 metres skyward, visible across the city and thrillingly close from the Eaux-Vives jetty.
St. Pierre Cathedral
John Calvin preached the Reformation beneath these austere Gothic vaults; climb the towers for the finest panorama of lake, rooftops and Mont Blanc.
Old Town and Place du Bourg-de-Four
Europe's diplomacy capital hides a charming medieval core whose oldest square, a former Roman market, buzzes with café terraces beneath shuttered townhouses.
Palais des Nations
The vast Art Deco headquarters of the UN in Europe offers guided tours past the Assembly Hall and the famous Broken Chair sculpture opposite its gates.
Reformation Wall (Mur des Réformateurs)
Ten-metre granite figures of Calvin, Knox and fellow reformers stand in stern relief along Bastions Park beneath the old city ramparts.
Flower Clock (L'Horloge Fleurie)
Planted with 6,500 seasonal blooms in the Jardin Anglais, this working timepiece charmingly salutes Geneva's twin obsessions of horology and horticulture.
Bains des Pâquis
This beloved 1930s lakeside lido juts into the harbour, where locals swim, sauna and eat fondue with front-row views of the Jet d'Eau.
CERN Science Gateway
At the world's largest physics laboratory, striking Renzo Piano-designed pavilions and the iconic Globe demystify the Large Hadron Collider and the birth of the web.
International Red Cross and Red Crescent Museum
A moving, superbly curated museum on humanitarian action, from Henry Dunant's founding vision to interactive exhibits confronting today's crises.
Carouge
Built by Sardinian kings as a rival town, this Mediterranean-flavored quarter of low ochre houses, artisan boutiques and leafy courtyards feels like Italy in Geneva.

train.note: Geneva Cornavin is one of Europe's better-connected stations for its size, and the Léman Express regional network makes cross-border travel into Haute-Savoie as easy as a metro ride. TGV Lyria reaches Paris in about 3h10 and the EuroCity to Milan takes 4. Note that Geneva Airport station is one stop from Cornavin and many international trains call there. Swiss fares are cheapest as Supersaver tickets, released about two months ahead.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the Gare Routière de Genève on Place Dorcière, near the lake. Chamonix is about 90 minutes away by direct shuttle, and ski transfers run heavily in winter. Geneva is almost surrounded by France, so many local TPG bus routes cross the border - carry your passport or ID card.

intl.to: Lausanne, Montreux, Évian & Thonon-les-Bains (Switzerland/France) - Lake Geneva boats

ferry.note: CGN's Lake Geneva boats are a genuine international service - Évian and Thonon are in France - and are covered by Swiss rail passes. The Nyon-Yvoire and Lausanne-Évian crossings are used by commuters as well as visitors. Sailings are far more frequent between April and October, with the historic paddle steamers running mainly in summer. Geneva's own mouettes are little yellow water taxis across the harbour on an ordinary transit ticket.

half.name: Chamonix & Mont Blanc
half.blurb: Alpine resort town beneath Western Europe's highest peak, with cable cars climbing to glacier viewpoints.

half.name: Montreux & Château de Chillon
half.blurb: Lakeside town on Lake Geneva anchored by a moated medieval castle rising directly from the water.

half.name: Annecy
half.blurb: Alpine town built around canals and a turquoise lake, its old quarter often called the Venice of the Alps.

half.name: Gruyères
half.blurb: Hilltop medieval village and namesake of the famous cheese, with a castle and views over green Fribourg countryside.
